48.2. One exact residual identity for Eulerian/material composition

Fix the common root data. Let eta be a stipulated smooth
volume-preserving path, eta(0)=id, V=eta_t, V(0)=u0. Put
  u=V o eta^(-1), p=pi o eta^(-1),
  F=D_a eta, A=F^(-1), mean(pi)=0.

Define the actual residuals

  R_E(u,p):=u_t+(u dot grad)u+grad p-nu Delta u,
  R_M(eta,pi):=eta_tt+A^T grad_a pi
                   -nu Div_a(D_a eta_t A A^T).

ID03 supplies Piola, and ID04 supplies the differentiated composition
identities. Substituting their literal right sides gives

  R_M(eta,pi)
   =[(u_t+(u dot grad)u) o eta]+[(grad p) o eta]
                                        -nu[(Delta u) o eta]
   =R_E(u,p) o eta.                                       (48.1)

The order D_a eta_t A A^T is unchanged. Since eta is onto,

  R_M(eta,pi)=0 <-> R_E(u,p)=0.                            (48.2)

Moreover ID02 gives
  mean(pi)=mean(p),
  ||eta_t||_2=||u||_2,
  int |D_a eta_t A|^2 da=int |D_xu|^2 dx.
Initial data transfer by eta(0)=id and V(0)=u0. Thus (48.2) is a
composition of exact predicates with their gauges and initial data;
it does not compare unnormalized equations alone.

The literal source route is:
  ML-O product/chain/matrix specializations in ID01--ID04;
  quotient-measure identification in ID02/ID16;
  ML-I02 after the proved measure-preserving equivalence;
  (48.1)--(48.2).

48.3. The pressure-free residual and the variational composition

Let
  r=u_t+B(u,u)-nu Delta u,
  P the full-mean Leray projection, P_0=I,
  P_eta=U_eta P U_eta^(-1).

ID06--ID07 prove, with actual constant and transverse real Fourier
tests and uniform smooth coefficient reconstruction,

  P r=0
    <-> exists! p smooth, mean(p)=0, r=-grad p.             (48.3)

ID15 then gives the exact projected equation

  P_eta eta_tt=nu Delta_eta eta_t
    <-> P r=0.                                            (48.4)

For an endpoint-fixed smooth solenoidal virtual displacement w, set
W=w o eta. Define the action and Rayleigh function on the material
configuration and its velocity as in Sections 8--9. ID08--ID09 give

  delta u=w_t+[u,w],
  delta S_eta[W]-int_0^T D_V R(eta,V)[W]dt
    =-int_0^T int_Omega r dot w dx dt.                     (48.5)

The derivative D_V R is at fixed eta and is evaluated on W, as the
velocity-fibre direction representing the virtual displacement. It is
not evaluated on delta u or on W_t. The pressure term has zero pairing
with every such displacement by div w=0 and periodic integration.

Temporal localization followed by the spatial testing result in ID06
turns vanishing of the right side of (48.5) for every w into P r=0 at
each interior time, then at both endpoints by continuity. Conversely
P r=0 annihilates every such test. Consequently

  actual material Lagrange-d'Alembert
    <-> reduced solenoidal virtual work
    <-> P r=0
    <-> normalized NSE.                                   (48.6)

The literal source route is:
  M01/M02/M04 and ML-I03 after the representation primitives
    ID16.1--ID16.3 and time primitives ID17.1--ID17.3
    (or direct finite-interval FTC);
  actual variation identities ID08--ID09;
  actual Fourier coefficient and smooth-pressure identities ID06--ID07;
  (48.3)--(48.6).

No all-positive-time NSE source predicate is introduced by this route.
ID17 supplies actual local test extensions when general source
differentiation theorems require all positive times.

48.4. Newtonian traction and exact root inverse laws

For sigma=-p I+nu(D_xu+D_xu^T), the finite coordinate calculation gives
  div sigma=-grad p+nu Delta u
when div u=0. ID05 supplies the independently derived region identities:

  d_t int_{eta(t,A0)}u dx=int_{eta(t,A0)}(u_t+B(u,u))dx,
  int_{boundary eta(t,A0)}sigma n dS
       =int_{eta(t,A0)}div sigma dx.

Thus the material-region balance defect is

  d_t int_{eta(t,A0)}u dx
    -int_{boundary eta(t,A0)}sigma n dS
      =int_{eta(t,A0)}R_E(u,p)dx.                          (48.7)

If this vanishes for every stipulated smooth region A0, use the inverse
flow to choose arbitrary sufficiently small current coordinate balls.
The integral average tends to R_E(t,x) by continuity, hence R_E=0.
The reverse implication follows by integrating the zero residual.
The gauge, initial data and incompressibility are already common to
the two solution predicates. Therefore E=N as sets of pairs.

The remaining exact maps are

  Phi_T:E -> M,
    Phi_T(u,p)=(eta_u,p o eta_u),
  Psi_T:M -> E,
    Psi_T(eta,pi)=(eta_t o eta^(-1),pi o eta^(-1)).

Direct substitution and uniqueness of the identity-normalized flow give

  Psi_T o Phi_T=id_E,
  Phi_T o Psi_T=id_M.                                     (48.8)

For the reduced class V, forget the normalized pressure in the forward
map and use the unique pressure in (48.3) in the reverse map. For D,
forget material pressure in the forward map; (48.5)--(48.6) and the
same unique reconstruction supply the inverse. Hence the exact root is

  E=N,                 E ~= M ~= D,                 E ~= V. (48.9)

All maps commute with restriction from [0,T] to [0,S], 0<S<=T: flow
uniqueness identifies the restrictions, and pressure reconstruction is
pointwise in time with the same spatial zero-mean gauge. The maps
preserve the kinetic energy and dissipation by ID02 and ID04.

49.0 EXACT DATA, NOTATION, AND QUANTIFIERS

Fix nu>0, 0<T<infinity, Omega=R^3/Z^3 with normalized volume, and a
stipulated root solution (u,p) on [0,T]xOmega:

 u_t+B(u,u)+grad p−nu Delta u=0,   div u=0,
 u(0)=u0,                         integral_Omega p(t)=0.       (49.0)

The root smoothness convention is unchanged: all stated derivatives
extend continuously to the finite slab, time derivatives at endpoints
are interpreted one-sided, and spatial representatives are smooth
periodic functions. The bilinear differential expression is
 B(f,g)=(f·grad)g, with (D_xg)_{ij}=partial_j g_i.
Neither mean u0 nor the mean of a supplemental initial variation is
assumed zero. No root existence or continuation assertion is introduced.

Let eta be the identity-normalized flow of u. Set

 V=eta_t=u o eta,     pi=p o eta,     F=D_a eta,
 A=F^{-1},           J=det F=1,      G=A A^T,
 B_eta=(D_xu) o eta=D_aV A,
 D_j^eta=sum_alpha A_{alpha j} partial_{a_alpha},
 grad_eta theta=A^T grad_a theta,
 div_eta H=tr(D_aH A),
 Delta_eta H=Div_a(D_aH G)=sum_j D_j^eta D_j^eta H.

Div acts on matrix rows. The notation B_eta for the matrix is distinct
from the two-input differential expression B(f,g). Pullback U_eta f=f o
eta acts on scalar components or vector components as stated; a
covector pullback is not substituted for this componentwise operation.

For a variation parameter s in an open interval containing 0, delta
denotes partial_s at s=0. Define

 W=delta eta,  Z=delta V=W_t,  rho=delta pi,
 H=D_aW,       M=H A,          j=tr(H A),
 w=W o eta^{-1},  z=delta u,    q=delta p.

An actual family in ID40 is a jointly smooth family of periodic
orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms eta_s(t), with eta_s(0)=id,
and smooth periodic material scalars pi_s. Set V_s=partial_t eta_s,
u_s=V_s o eta_s^{-1}, p_s=pi_s o eta_s^{-1}. Volume preservation and
pressure normalization are imposed exactly where stated. The family
need not satisfy NSE. The base s=0 may also be taken off shell in the
explicit identities of ID41; that assertion states its broader data
separately and does not alter the root theorem.

For any prescribed smooth solenoidal h0, the linearized initial datum
z(0)=h0 is a supplemental varying-datum problem. The original fixed-u0
root has h0=0. This distinction is retained in every converse and in
the final uniqueness statement.

L40.a. Matrix, determinant, and inverse-map variations.

For the actual family specified in 49.0, every fixed (t,a) satisfies

 delta F=H,
 delta A=−A H A,
 delta J=J tr(AH),
 delta G=−A H G−G H^T A^T.                                (49.1)

At the volume-preserving base J=1, delta J=j. If zeta_s=eta_s^{-1},

 delta zeta(t,x)=−[A W](t,zeta(t,x)).                      (49.2)

Proof. Smooth mixed-derivative symmetry gives delta F=D_aW. The
invertible matrix F represents a continuous linear equivalence of
EuclideanSpace R (Fin 3). ML-J01, with order infinity and this
equivalence, gives smoothness of its inverse along the actual family.
Differentiate AF=I by the component product rule and multiply on the
right by A:
 (delta A)F+AH=0, hence delta A=−AHA.
The displayed formula for delta G follows by differentiating AA^T.

For the determinant, ML-O11 expands det F into its six degree-three
monomials. Differentiating them with ML-O12 gives
 delta J=sum_{i,alpha} cof(F)_{i alpha} H_{i alpha}.
The inverse/cofactor identities from ID02--ID03 turn this sum into
J tr(AH). This derivation is valid before setting J=1. ML-J02, with
c(s)=J_s(t,a), c'=delta J and c(0)>0, also gives
 delta(J^{-1})=−delta J/J^2.                              (49.3)
Finally differentiate eta_s(t,zeta_s(t,x))=x. The two terms are
W(t,zeta)+F(t,zeta)delta zeta, proving (49.2). Smoothness of the
parameter-dependent inverse follows either from the inverse-map
construction in ID01 or from the spacetime-parameter inverse map
(s,t,a)↦(s,t,eta_s(t,a)); its derivative has invertible diagonal block F.

L40.b. Actual Eulerian variations and the kinematic equation.

For any jointly smooth scalar or vector family f_s,

 delta(f_s o eta_s)=(delta f_s) o eta+(D_x f o eta)W.       (49.4)

Applying this to u_s and p_s proves the exact inverse formulas

 Z=z o eta+B_eta W,                    W_t=B_eta W+z o eta,
 rho=q o eta+(grad p o eta)·W,
 z=(Z−B_eta W) o eta^{-1},
 q=[rho−(grad_eta pi)·W] o eta^{-1}.                       (49.5)

In Eulerian displacement variables these are

 z=w_t+B(u,w)−B(w,u),
 q=rho o eta^{-1}−w·grad p.                              (49.6)

Proof. Equation (49.4) is the chain rule applied to the parameter
curve s↦(s,eta_s(t,a)). Since W=w o eta, its time derivative is
W_t=[w_t+B(u,w)] o eta. Comparing with the first formula in (49.5)
gives (49.6). Mixed partials give Z=W_t. No field equation enters.
At t=0, eta_s(0)=id gives W(0)=0 and therefore z(0)=Z(0).
If V_s(0)=u0+s h0+o(s), then Z(0)=h0. If V_s(0)=u0 for every s,
then h0=0.

ML-O19 = HasFDerivAt.mul
ML-O20 = HasFDerivAt.fun_sum

For (49.6), apply the same chain rule to t↦(t,eta(t,a)).
[END_LEAN_ENDPOINT_INDEX]

L40.c. Infinitesimal incompressibility and its propagation.

The matrix M equals (D_xw) o eta, by differentiating W=w o eta.
Consequently

 j=div_eta W=(div w) o eta.                              (49.7)

If the actual family is volume preserving, then j=0. Conversely,
for any smooth W with W(0)=0, define Z=W_t and z by (49.5). At the
solenoidal base, direct differentiation gives

 j_t=tr(D_aZ A−D_aV A H A)=(div z) o eta.                 (49.8)

Indeed A_t=−A(D_aV)A and cyclicity of the finite trace give the first
equality. For the second, differentiate (49.6) in x. For all smooth
u,w,

 div(B(u,w)−B(w,u))
   =u·grad(div w)−w·grad(div u),

because the two products of first derivatives are equal after exchanging
their summed indices. Thus div z=(partial_t+u·grad)div w when div u=0.
Compose with eta to obtain (49.8). In particular,

 [W(0)=0 and div z=0]  iff  [W(0)=0 and div_eta W=0].      (49.9)

The reverse implication differentiates the identity j=0; the forward
implication integrates j_t=0 with j(0)=0. Equivalently, the linearized
velocity constraint is

 delta[div_{eta_s} V_s]
   =tr(D_aZ A−D_aV A H A)=0.                             (49.10)

The equivalence is asserted under the kinematic relation (49.5).
It is not an equivalence between unrelated choices of W and z.

[LEAN_ENDPOINT_INDEX]
ML-R02 = intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDerivAt_of_le
Specialization: for each fixed label a use the real curve j(t,a),
the derivative in (49.8), and endpoints 0<=t<=T. Continuity on Icc
and the interior derivative hypotheses follow from the smooth fields.
[END_LEAN_ENDPOINT_INDEX]

L40.d. Correct pressure normalization under motion.

At the volume-preserving base the change of variables in ID02 and
periodic integration by parts give

 integral rho
   =integral q+integral (grad p)·w
   =integral q−integral p div w
   =integral q−integral pi j.                            (49.11)

Therefore, for tangent variations j=0,

 integral rho=0  iff  integral q=0.                       (49.12)

For a family that is not volume preserving, the correct differentiated
normalization is instead

 delta integral_Omega p_s
   =delta integral_Omega pi_s J_s
   =integral (rho+pi j)=integral q                       (49.13)

at J=1. This retains the moving-volume factor. A replacement of the
physical pressure variation q by rho o eta^{-1} would omit the term
w·grad p and generally violate (49.5).

Proof of the integral differentiation. On any compact s-subinterval
around 0, all integrands and their s-derivatives are uniformly bounded
on the compact torus. The fundamental theorem of calculus in s makes
the difference quotient a bounded average of the derivative; uniform
continuity gives uniform convergence to that derivative. Passing the
uniform limit through the finite-volume integral proves (49.13).
ML-K02 provides the same derivative-under-integral endpoint with the
uniform bound as its integrable dominating function. M01 applied to
the smooth periodic products p w_j proves the integration by parts
in (49.11); when j=0, M04 applies directly to (w,p).

M01 = SingularClosure.critical_integral_real_directionalDerivative_eq_zero
M04 = SingularClosure.critical_smooth_integral_inner_gradient_eq_zero
Specialization: the measurable equivalence is the actual flow eta;
the parameter for ML-K02 is s, the measure is finite torus volume,
and the scalar integrand is pi_s J_s. All M01/M04 uses are individual
smooth periodic spatial slices. ID17 supplies the finite-time convention.
[END_LEAN_ENDPOINT_INDEX]

L41.a. Residual conjugacy before imposing the equation.

For this identity only, let (u,p) be any jointly smooth periodic pair;
no equation or divergence constraint is needed. Let eta be its actual
identity-normalized flow, J>0, and V=u o eta, pi=p o eta. Define

 R_E(u,p)=u_t+B(u,u)+grad p−nu Delta u,
 Delta_eta^J H=J^{-1} Div_a(J D_aH A A^T),
 R_M^J(eta,pi)=eta_tt+A^T grad_a pi−nu Delta_eta^J eta_t.

The material chain rule, Piola identity, and gradient identity give

 R_M^J(eta,pi)=R_E(u,p) o eta.                            (49.14)

These are identities on the actual finite slab. The off-shell field
need not have a volume-preserving flow; the displayed Jacobian factors
are retained. At a solenoidal base J=1 this agrees with the material
residual used in the root theorem.

Now take any actual smooth family as in 49.0, or its equivalent
Eulerian family of fields and flows. Define z,q,W,Z,rho by ID40. The
Eulerian residual derivative is

 L_u(z,q)=z_t+B(u,z)+B(z,u)+grad q−nu Delta z.              (49.15)

For example, in components,
 delta(sum_j u_{s,j} partial_j u_{s,i})
   =sum_j[z_j partial_j u_i+u_j partial_j z_i].
Smoothness commutes delta with partial_t, gradient, and Laplacian.
This proves (49.15), including its actual interpretation as a derivative.

product rule. No L2-boundedness assertion for B is used.
[END_LEAN_ENDPOINT_INDEX]

L41.b. Differential of the material pressure and viscosity.

Return to a solenoidal base, so J=1, but initially allow the family
itself to have arbitrary first volume variation j. Set

 g=grad_eta pi,    dotG=−A H G−G H^T A^T.

Differentiating the pressure term gives

 delta(grad_{eta_s} pi_s)=grad_eta rho−M^T g.              (49.16)

Using (49.1), (49.3), and the product rule on the full J-weighted
Laplacian gives

 delta(Delta_{eta_s}^{J_s} V_s)
  =−j Delta_eta V+Div_a(j D_aV G+D_aZ G+D_aV dotG)
  =Delta_eta Z+Div_a(D_aV dotG)+(D_aV G)grad_a j.           (49.17)

The last equality is a rowwise product rule. It explains exactly why
the final term disappears for a tangent direction j=0, and why that
term cannot be discarded for an arbitrary deformation.

An independent differential-operator form is useful for checking every
coefficient. From delta A=−AHA and M=D_aW A,

 delta D_j^eta=−sum_k M_{k j}D_k^eta.

Commuting the pulled-back coordinate derivatives gives, for each vector
component of V,

 delta(Delta_{eta_s}^{J_s} V_s)
  =Delta_eta Z
   −2 sum_{j,k} M_{k j}D_j^eta D_k^eta V
   −sum_{j,k}(D_j^eta M_{k j})D_k^eta V.                 (49.18)

For this calculation, expand delta(D_j^eta D_j^eta V), apply the
operator product rule twice, and use D_j^eta D_k^eta=D_k^eta D_j^eta.
The equality of the derivatives follows from their actual conjugacy to
partial_j and partial_k, not from a constant-coefficient assumption.
Formula (49.18) is valid for an arbitrary first deformation; (49.17)
and (49.18) are equal because the full Piola Laplacian is the same
operator. The j term in (49.17) is contained in the derivative-of-M
terms after conversion between divergence and coordinate forms.

These identities can also be checked directly in Eulerian variables.
The formulas Z=[z+B(w,u)] o eta, M=(D_xw) o eta give

 delta(Delta_{eta_s}^{J_s} V_s)
    =(Delta z) o eta+(D_x Delta u o eta)W.               (49.19)

Indeed expand Delta[z+(D_xu)w]. The terms
2 sum_{j,k}(partial_j w_k)partial_j partial_k u and
sum_k(Delta w_k)partial_k u cancel the two sums in (49.18).
The remaining terms are Delta z+(D_x Delta u)w.
Similarly, writing rho=[q+w·grad p] o eta, expanding its material
gradient, and using symmetry of D_x^2p gives

 grad_eta rho−M^T g
    =(grad q) o eta+(D_x grad p o eta)W.                 (49.20)

Here the derivative falling on w produces M^T g and is canceled
explicitly. These checks identify the pressure and viscous variations
as physical variations at a moving point.

L41.c. Acceleration variation and exact differentiated conjugacy.

Let a=u_t+B(u,u). Differentiate Z=z o eta+B_eta W in time and use
W_t=z o eta+B_eta W. The result is

 Z_t=[z_t+B(u,z)+B(z,u)] o eta+(D_xa o eta)W.             (49.21)

For the last coefficient, the product rule gives
 (B_eta)_t+B_eta^2=(D_xa) o eta.
In coordinates the second derivatives of u commute, so differentiating
D_xu along u equals the part of D_x[(D_xu)u] in which the derivative
falls on D_xu; the remaining part is (D_xu)^2. This verifies (49.21).

Define at the solenoidal base the full derivative expression

 DcalM_eta,pi[W,rho]
  =W_tt+grad_eta rho−M^T grad_eta pi
    −nu[Delta_eta W_t+Div_a(D_aV dotG)+(D_aV G)grad_a j]. (49.22)

Adding (49.19)--(49.21) proves

 DcalM_eta,pi[W,rho]
    =[L_u(z,q)] o eta+(D_x R_E(u,p) o eta)W.             (49.23)

The same equation follows by differentiating (49.14) with its full J
dependence. The second term is the exact off-shell defect term. It is
the derivative of the residual caused by varying the evaluation point.
It is not generally zero, even when the Eulerian variation solves
L_u(z,q)=0 about an off-shell pair.

For a volume-preserving family, j=0. The material tangent operator is
therefore

 calL_eta,pi(W,rho)
  =W_tt+grad_eta rho−(D_aW A)^T grad_eta pi
    −nu[Delta_eta W_t+Div_a(D_aV dotG)],
 dotG=−A(D_aW)G−G(D_aW)^T A^T.                          (49.24)

At the stipulated root R_E=0, its spatial derivative is zero. Thus

 calL_eta,pi(W,rho)=U_eta L_u(z,q)                       (49.25)

for every smooth tangent pair linked by (49.5). Identity (49.25) is
proved for actual kinematic tangents in ID40 and, by the realization
in ID42 below, for every pair in the precisely defined tangent spaces.

L41.d. Polarized spatial flux and the pressure compatibility.

For solenoidal u,z define the symmetric tensor
 T_{ij}=u_i z_j+z_i u_j. The mixed product rule gives

 B(u,z)+B(z,u)=div T,
 div[B(u,z)+B(z,u)]=2 tr(D_xu D_xz).                     (49.26)

To prove the first identity, differentiate each tensor entry. The
terms u_i div z and z_i div u vanish. For the second, first derivatives
of div u and div z vanish; the two remaining double sums coincide
after exchanging their indices. Periodic integration then gives
integral tr(D_xu D_xz)=0.

L42.a. Exact two linearized solution sets.

For a fixed smooth solenoidal h0, define E_lin(h0) to consist of all
jointly smooth periodic pairs (z,q) on the stipulated slab satisfying

 L_u(z,q)=0,      div z=0,
 z(0)=h0,        integral q(t)=0.                        (49.27)

Define M_lin(h0) to consist of all jointly smooth periodic material
pairs (W,rho) satisfying

 calL_eta,pi(W,rho)=0,       div_eta W=0,
 W(0)=0,                   W_t(0)=h0,
 integral rho(t)=0.                                      (49.28)

W is a vector field along the fixed base eta, represented by its
periodic lift. It is not assumed itself to be a diffeomorphism. These
definitions introduce no nonemptiness premise for h0 other than the
explicit zero solution when h0=0.

The forward map E_lin(h0)→M_lin(h0) is the explicit formula

 W(t,a)=F(t,a) integral_0^t A(s,a)z(s,eta(s,a)) ds,
 rho=q o eta+(grad_eta pi)·W.                            (49.29)

The reverse map is

 z=[W_t−B_eta W] o eta^{-1},
 q=[rho−(grad_eta pi)·W] o eta^{-1}.                      (49.30)

L42.b. Existence-independent reconstruction and inverse identities.

Let z be any smooth solenoidal field on the slab, without assuming a
linearized PDE. Formula (49.29) defines a smooth W. Smoothness follows
by differentiating the finite integral, using uniform bounds for every
derivative on the compact slab. The proof of the time derivative is
the fundamental theorem of calculus; spatial derivatives follow from
the difference-quotient/dominated-integral argument used in ID07.
At endpoints the same argument uses the one-sided time primitive.

Since F_t=B_eta F and FA=I, direct differentiation gives

 W_t=B_eta W+z o eta,
 W(0)=0,   W_t(0)=z(0).                                 (49.31)

If another W obeys the same equation and initial value, multiply by A:
 (AW)_t=A(z o eta). Integrating proves (49.29), hence uniqueness.
Equation (49.8) now gives div_eta W=0. Conversely, for any W with
div_eta W=0 and W(0)=0, the z defined by (49.30) is solenoidal,
and the same integration of (AW)_t reconstructs the original W.
The scalar formulas in (49.29)--(49.30) cancel directly, and their
normalized gauges are equivalent by (49.12).

Apply (49.25). The material equation is equivalent to the Eulerian
linearized equation because U_eta has inverse U_eta^{-1}. Initial
values match by F(0)=A(0)=I and W(0)=0. This proves that (49.29) and
(49.30) are mutually inverse bijections between (49.27) and (49.28).

There is also an actual kinematic realization of every smooth pair
(z,q) with div z=0 and integral q=0, whether or not it solves (49.27).
For |s| sufficiently small, set

 u_s=u+s z,       p_s=p+s q,
 eta_s=the identity-normalized flow of u_s,
 pi_s=p_s o eta_s.                                      (49.32)

Each u_s is divergence free, hence eta_s is volume preserving. Each
p_s has normalized mean. On a fixed bounded s-interval all spatial
derivatives of u_s are uniformly bounded on the compact slab, so the
finite-slab flow proof of ID01 applies uniformly; its parameter
variation proof gives joint smoothness and the variational equation
(49.31). Thus delta eta_s=W and delta pi_s=rho exactly.
The initial velocity is u_s(0)=u0+s h0 when z(0)=h0. In the original
fixed-datum case h0=0, this family has initial velocity exactly u0.

The family (49.32) is a family of kinematic fields and flows. Its
members are not asserted to solve NSE. A bijection of linearized
solution sets does not establish that every element integrates to a
nonlinear NSE solution family. The reconstruction requires only a
stipulated z, not a new NSE existence theorem.

L42.c. Exact normalized linearized pressure and projected equation.

Let z be a stipulated smooth solenoidal field, and put
 c_u,z=B(u,z)+B(z,u). For this paragraph c_u,z denotes the field,
not the constant variation mean used below. Define q_z by its actual
Fourier coefficients:

 qhat_z(0)=0,
 qhat_z(k)=−[k·chat_u,z(k)]/[2*pi*i*|k|^2],  k!=0.        (49.33)

The smooth pressure reconstruction of ID07 proves that this defines
an actual smooth real periodic scalar, jointly smooth on the slab.
For completeness, repeated integration by parts gives for every
ell,N a uniform bound
 (1+4*pi^2|k|^2)^N |partial_t^ell chat_u,z(k)|<=C_{ell,N}
on [0,T]. This follows by integrating the smooth field
(1−Delta)^N partial_t^ell c_u,z on the unit cube. These constants
are finite by compactness. Multiplication by k/|k|^2 in (49.33)
preserves faster-than-polynomial decay away from k=0; every mixed
derivative series is uniformly absolutely convergent. The termwise
derivative argument of ID07 proves the asserted joint smoothness.
The coefficients satisfy conjugate symmetry, so q_z is real.

If Q=I−P is the full Leray complementary projection, including
P(0)=I, the coefficient formula gives

 grad q_z=−Q c_u,z,
 −Delta q_z=div c_u,z=2 tr(D_xu D_xz),
 integral q_z=0.                                        (49.34)

Equivalently, with T from (49.26),

 qhat_z(k)=−sum_{i,j} k_i k_j That_{ij}(k)/|k|^2
 for k!=0.                                              (49.35)

The zero coefficient is zero. The Poisson compatibility follows from
the integral identity in (49.26). If two normalized pressures have the
same gradient, their difference has zero derivative on the connected
periodic lift, so ML-O21 makes it spatially constant; its mean makes
that constant zero.

Consequently, for a smooth solenoidal z,

 [there exists normalized q with L_u(z,q)=0]
   iff z_t+P c_u,z−nu Delta z=0,                         (49.36)

and such q equals q_z. The forward direction applies P, using that
P fixes z_t and Delta z and annihilates gradients. The reverse
direction inserts (49.34). Constant velocity modes are retained;
the projection in (49.36) is not the mean-zero projection.

L42.d. Variation mean, strain identity, and the correct gap estimate.

Let (z,q) satisfy (49.27). Periodic integration of its equation gives

 integral z(t)=integral h0=:c.                           (49.37)

Indeed the mixed convection is div T by (49.26), and the gradient
and Laplacian also have zero periodic integral. The material mean
has the same value:

 integral W_t=integral z=c.                              (49.38)

To verify (49.38), integrate W_t=[z+B(w,u)] o eta. Change variables
and use div w=0 to obtain integral B(w,u)=0. Thus the material and
Eulerian variation means agree; neither is silently set to zero.

Let S_u=(D_xu+(D_xu)^T)/2 and define the continuous finite function

 a_u(t)=max_{x in Omega, |xi|=1} [−xi^T S_u(t,x)xi].

This is the exact best pointwise upper bound on the quadratic form
−xi^T S_u xi. Compactness gives the maximum, and uniform continuity
of S_u proves continuity of a_u. Pairing (49.27) with z yields

 (1/2) d_t ||z||_2^2+nu||D_xz||_2^2
     =−integral z^T S_u z.                              (49.39)

The transport term integral z·B(u,z) is the integral of
u·grad(|z|^2/2) and vanishes. The pressure term vanishes because
div z=0; the Laplacian term is the periodic gradient square. The
antisymmetric part of D_xu has zero quadratic form. It follows that

 ||z(t)||_2<=exp(integral_s^t a_u)||z(s)||_2,
 0<=s<=t<=T.                                            (49.40)

This estimate holds with arbitrary c and arbitrary base mean.
Explicitly, (49.39) gives d_t||z||_2^2<=2a_u||z||_2^2.
The derivative of exp(−2 integral_s^t a_u)||z(t)||_2^2 is nonpositive;
finite-interval FTC and the nonnegative square root give (49.40).

For the sharper mean-zero estimate, write b=z−c. Its exact equation is

 b_t+B(u,b)+B(b,u)+grad q−nu Delta b=−B(c,u),
 integral b=0.                                          (49.41)

Set lambda_1=4*pi^2, alpha=a_u−nu lambda_1, and
 beta=||B(c,u)||_2<=|c| ||D_xu||_2.
With Y=||b||_2^2, periodic Poincare and (49.41) give

 (1/2)Y'<=alpha Y+beta sqrt(Y).                          (49.42)

The Poincare constant lambda_1 is exact for the unit torus: Parseval
gives ||D_xb||_2^2=sum_{k!=0}4*pi^2|k|^2|bhat(k)|^2,
and the first nonzero Fourier shell attains the universal bound.
The strain coefficient and this Poincare constant are sharp in their
stated separate senses; simultaneous equality is not asserted.

For all s<=t define E_alpha(t,s)=exp(integral_s^t alpha). Then

 ||b(t)||_2<=E_alpha(t,s)||b(s)||_2
              +integral_s^t E_alpha(t,tau)beta(tau)dtau. (49.43)

Proof at possible zeroes of b. For epsilon>0 let
y_epsilon=sqrt(Y+epsilon^2). Direct differentiation gives
y_epsilon'<=alpha y_epsilon+beta+epsilon|alpha|.
The last term follows from −alpha epsilon^2/y_epsilon<=epsilon|alpha|
and is necessary when alpha is negative. Multiply by the integrating
factor, integrate its actual derivative inequality, and let epsilon
decrease to zero. Since 0<=y_epsilon−sqrt Y<=epsilon and alpha is
bounded on the finite slab, the extra integral tends uniformly to zero.
This proves (49.43) without division by sqrt Y.

If c=0, beta=0 and (49.43) becomes the homogeneous sharp-gap bound

 ||z(t)||_2<=exp(integral_s^t[a_u−nu lambda_1])||z(s)||_2. (49.44)

For c!=0, the forcing term in (49.41)--(49.43) is retained. A
homogeneous version of (49.44) for ||z−c||_2 is not a consequence.

L42.e. Fixed-datum specialization and an explicit nonzero-mean family.

If h0=0, (49.40) gives z=0. Equation (49.27) then gives grad q=0;
its mean gives q=0. Formula (49.29) gives W=0 and rho=0. More generally,
subtracting two solutions of (49.27) with the same h0 and applying
this argument proves uniqueness, and the material bijection transfers
that uniqueness to (49.28).

Thus the homogeneous linearized tangent at a stipulated smooth root
with its original initial datum fixed is the zero tangent. Nonzero
h0 belongs to the explicitly varying-datum supplemental problem.

There is a useful exact nonlinear family for a particular class of
nonzero-mean directions. For any constant c in R^3, define

 u^s(t,x)=u(t,x−s c t)+s c,
 p^s(t,x)=p(t,x−s c t),
 eta^s(t,a)=eta(t,a)+s c t.                              (49.45)

The terms −s(c·grad)u from the time derivative and +s(c·grad)u from
convection cancel. Spatial derivatives and translations commute, so
(u^s,p^s) is a root-form NSE pair with initial datum u0+s c and the
same viscosity and finite slab. Translation preserves pressure mean.
The flow identity follows by substituting eta^s in u^s. Its tangent is

 z_c=c−t(c·grad)u,      q_c=−t(c·grad)p,
 W_c=t c,              (W_c)_t=c,           rho_c=0.       (49.46)

These formulas satisfy (49.27)--(49.30) with h0=c. In particular,
z_c−c=−t(c·grad)u can be nonzero despite having zero initial value.
This directly verifies the necessity of the forcing in (49.41).
The explicit Galilean family is an integrability statement only for
these particular directions; it does not imply integrability of all
linearized solutions into nonlinear families.

maps, actual off-shell kinematic realization, unique normalized pressure,
the mean-sensitive energy estimates, and the original fixed-datum
zero-tangent specialization.

50.0. Quantified common data and conventions

Fix \(\nu>0\), \(0<T<\infty\), \(I=[0,T]\), and
\(\Omega=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3\) with normalized volume \(dx\).
All smooth fields below have the root's joint time-space regularity,
including continuous one-sided derivatives of every order at 0 and T.
No extension of a fluid solution beyond I is a hypothesis.

Let
\[
 \mathcal H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3),\qquad
 \mathcal H_\sigma=\{f\in\mathcal H:\operatorname{div}f=0
                                      \text{ distributionally}\},
 \quad \mathcal H_0=\{f:\overline f=0\}.
\]
A subscript \(\sigma,0\) denotes the intersection. Put
\[
 \widehat f(k)=\int_\Omega e^{-2\pi i k\cdot x}f(x)\,dx,\quad
 \kappa_k=4\pi^2|k|^2,\quad \lambda_1=4\pi^2.
\]
The actual Leray multiplier is
\[
 P_0=I_{\mathbb R^3},\qquad
 P_k=I-\frac{kk^{\mathsf T}}{|k|^2}\ (k\ne0),\qquad Q=I-P.
                                                               \tag{50.1}
\]
Thus constants remain in \(\mathcal H_\sigma\). Every time integral is
a Bochner interval integral with respect to real Lebesgue measure; its
smooth pointwise and coefficient realizations are identified below.

The auxiliary forcing \(r\) in C60--C61 is stipulated smooth with
\(Pr=r\); its mean is unrestricted. This covers exactly the projected
residual of every supplied smooth divergence-free approximate field.
The unforced root is recovered by the specialization \(r=0\).

50.1.1. The actual bounded operators and their differential domain

For \(h\ge0\), define \(S_\nu(h):\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) by
\[
 \widehat{S_\nu(h)f}(k)=e^{-\nu\kappa_kh}\widehat f(k).       \tag{50.2}
\]
The right side is square summable, has the reality relation at k and
\(-k\), and therefore reconstructs one actual real L2 field. Parseval
gives bounded real linearity and
\[
 S_\nu(0)=I,\quad S_\nu(h+\ell)=S_\nu(h)S_\nu(\ell),\quad
 \|S_\nu(h)\|_{\mathcal H\to\mathcal H}=1,\quad
 PS_\nu(h)=S_\nu(h)P.                                     \tag{50.3}
\]
The norm equality is attained by a unit constant. The multiplier at
k=0 is exactly one; hence
\[
 \overline{S_\nu(h)f}=\overline f,\qquad
 \|S_\nu(h)|_{\mathcal H_0}\|=e^{-\nu\lambda_1h}.            \tag{50.4}
\]
The second equality is attained by a first-frequency real sine mode.
The same exact norm holds on \(\mathcal H_{\sigma,0}\), using
\(\sqrt2e_1\sin(2\pi x_2)\). The restrictions to the solenoidal spaces
are well defined by (50.3).

Finite Fourier sums prove strong continuity at every \(h\ge0\):
their coefficients are continuous, while the L2 error in a Fourier
tail is bounded uniformly by the original tail. The strong generator is
\[
 \nu\Delta,\qquad
 D(\Delta)=\left\{f:\sum_k\kappa_k^2|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\}
          =H^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).                        \tag{50.5}
\]
Indeed, for h>0,
\[
 \left|\frac{e^{-\nu\kappa h}-1}{h}\right|\le\nu\kappa .
\]
For f in the displayed domain, the weighted square-summable tail and
the finite-mode limit give the L2 derivative \(\nu\Delta f\) at zero.
Conversely, an L2 derivative g forces
\(\widehat g(k)=-\nu\kappa_k\widehat f(k)\) at every k, so f lies in
that domain. The derivative multipliers identify this weighted
domain with the actual weak-derivative H2 space, exactly as in ID21;
the full-vector real basis uses all three coordinate polarizations.
Restriction of (50.5) to \(\mathcal H_\sigma\) has domain \(H^2_\sigma\).

These are strong derivatives on the specified domain. No bounded
operator derivative at h=0 is asserted. The operator \(\Delta\) has
not been replaced by a bounded operator on \(\mathcal H\).

50.1.2. Uniform smooth reconstruction, including h=0

For any supplied jointly smooth field \(f:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3\),
every \(N,\ell\in\mathbb N\) admits a finite constant \(C_{N,\ell}\) with
\[
 \sup_{t\in I}|\partial_t^\ell\widehat f(t,k)|
       \le C_{N,\ell}(1+|k|)^{-N}.                        \tag{50.6}
\]
To derive this estimate, differentiate the coefficient integral on an
interior compact time neighborhood, where the continuous time
derivative is uniformly bounded. The same conclusion at endpoints
follows from the within-slab difference quotient and the uniform
continuity of that derivative. For k!=0 choose a coordinate j with
\(|k_j|\ge|k|/\sqrt3\) and integrate by parts N times in \(x_j\).
Periodicity cancels the boundary terms. The finitely many coordinate
choices share a compact-slab derivative bound; the k=0 coefficient
is separately bounded. This proves (50.6), also for every time
derivative and every smooth nonlinear field already defined from f.

The series \(\sum_k(1+|k|)^{-q}\) converges for q>3. Therefore, after
any fixed number of spatial derivatives and heat-parameter derivatives,
the series for \(S_\nu(h)f(t)\) is absolutely and uniformly convergent
on \(0\le h\le T,\ t\in I,\ x\in\Omega\): each heat derivative
contributes a factor \((-\nu\kappa_k)\), and the exponential remains
at most one. Choosing N larger than the resulting polynomial degree
plus three proves the required domination. Termwise differentiation
and continuous one-sided derivatives at h=0 follow from these
uniform derivative series and the one-variable FTC.

For a supplied smooth g and fixed s, define
\[
 d_k(t,s)=\int_s^t e^{-\nu\kappa_k(t-\tau)}\widehat g(\tau,k)\,d\tau,
                 \qquad 0\le s\le t\le T.                 \tag{50.7}
\]
Then
\[
 |d_k(t,s)|\le T\sup_{\tau\in I}|\widehat g(\tau,k)|,\quad
 \partial_t d_k=\widehat g(t,k)-\nu\kappa_kd_k,\quad
 \partial_s d_k=-e^{-\nu\kappa_k(t-s)}\widehat g(s,k).        \tag{50.8}
\]
For m>=1 the exact recurrence is
\[
 \partial_t^m d_k
  =\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}(-\nu\kappa_k)^j
             \partial_t^{m-1-j}\widehat g(t,k)
       +(-\nu\kappa_k)^m d_k.                             \tag{50.9}
\]
Differentiating the lower-endpoint formula gives the mixed s,t
derivatives. Equations (50.6)--(50.9) bound each derivative by a
polynomial in \(|k|\) times arbitrarily rapid decay, uniformly on
the closed triangle. Thus their Fourier sums and every fixed
derivative converge uniformly, including the diagonal t=s.

The corresponding Bochner integrand is continuous in \(\mathcal H\)
and bounded on the integration interval. Uniform smooth Fourier
convergence, or the continuity of every coefficient functional, gives
\[
 \widehat{\int_s^t S_\nu(t-\tau)g(\tau)\,d\tau}(k)=d_k(t,s).
                                                               \tag{50.10}
\]
In particular the Bochner and smooth pointwise realizations coincide.
No factor \(e^{+\nu\kappa_k\tau}\) is summed in this uniform argument.

50.1.3. The equivalence and its initial datum

Quantify arbitrary smooth \(f,g:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3\) and
\(f_0\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)\). Solenoidality is not needed
for this linear identity. The following predicates are equivalent:
\[
 \begin{split}
 {\rm (a)}\quad &f_t-\nu\Delta f=g \text{ on }I,\quad f(0)=f_0;\\
 {\rm (b)}\quad &f(t)=S_\nu(t)f_0+
          \int_0^tS_\nu(t-\tau)g(\tau)\,d\tau
                                    \quad(t\in I);\\
 {\rm (c)}\quad &f(0)=f_0,\quad
 f(t)=S_\nu(t-s)f(s)+
          \int_s^tS_\nu(t-\tau)g(\tau)\,d\tau
                                    \quad(0\le s\le t\le T).
 \end{split}                                               \tag{50.11}
\]
The equation in (a) uses one-sided derivatives at endpoints.

For (a) implies (c), every fixed Fourier mode satisfies
\[
 \partial_t\widehat f(t,k)+\nu\kappa_k\widehat f(t,k)
       =\widehat g(t,k).
\]
The scalar integrating factor gives
\[
 \partial_t\!\left(e^{\nu\kappa_kt}\widehat f(t,k)\right)
       =e^{\nu\kappa_kt}\widehat g(t,k).
\]
Integrate on [s,t], requiring derivatives only on (s,t) and continuous
endpoint values; divide by the positive scalar \(e^{\nu\kappa_kt}\).
The resulting coefficient equality is precisely the Fourier transform
of (c), by (50.10). Actual Fourier uniqueness proves the field equality.
The integrating-factor step is at a fixed k, where all quantities are
finite and continuous; (50.6)--(50.10) supply the separate uniform
reconstruction. Specializing s=0 proves (b).

For (b) implies (a), evaluate at t=0 to obtain the exact datum f0.
At every k rewrite its coefficient as
\[
 \widehat f(t,k)=e^{-\nu\kappa_kt}
  \left[\widehat f_0(k)+\int_0^t
                      e^{\nu\kappa_k\tau}\widehat g(\tau,k)\,d\tau\right].
                                                               \tag{50.12}
\]
Scalar FTC and the product rule give the mode differential equation
at each interior time. Fourier uniqueness and the actual Laplacian
coefficient identity recover \(f_t-\nu\Delta f=g\). All terms extend
continuously to the endpoints; equivalently the uniform derivative
calculation (50.8)--(50.9) gives the requisite right and left
derivatives there. This proves the endpoint equation as well.

For an independent restart calculation, apply \(S_\nu(t-s)\) to (b)
at time s, pass the fixed bounded linear map through the integral,
and use the semigroup law. Splitting the time-t integral at s yields
(c) by exact cancellation of the common integral over [0,s].
This uses only forward times; no inverse heat operator occurs.

At k=0, (50.11) gives the exact mean ledger
\[
 \overline f(t)=\overline f(s)+
                         \int_s^t\overline g(\tau)\,d\tau. \tag{50.13}
\]
The datum f0 is not removed when passing to restarted formulas.

50.2.1. Quantified data, pressure, and exact equivalent predicates

Fix \(u_0\in C^\infty_\sigma(\Omega)\), a supplied smooth
\(r:I\to C^\infty_\sigma(\Omega)\), and a supplied smooth
\(u:I\to C^\infty_\sigma(\Omega)\). The means of u0 and r are arbitrary.
Write \(c=B(u,u)=(u\cdot\nabla)u\), and define the actual normalized
pressure by
\[
 \widehat{q[u]}(0)=0,\qquad
 \widehat{q[u]}(k)=
       \frac{i\,k\cdot\widehat c(k)}{2\pi|k|^2}\quad(k\ne0).
                                                               \tag{50.14}
\]
The rapidly decreasing coefficients, the reality relation, and
(50.6) give a jointly smooth real pressure on the full closed slab.
Its exact gradient and gauge are
\[
 \nabla q[u]=-Qc,\qquad \int_\Omega q[u](t,x)\,dx=0.         \tag{50.15}
\]
The following predicates are equivalent:
\[
 \begin{split}
 {\rm (a)}\quad&
 \exists\,p\text{ smooth}:\quad
 u_t+c+\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=r,\quad u(0)=u_0,\quad
 \overline p=0;\\
 {\rm (b)}\quad&
 u_t+Pc-\nu\Delta u=r,\quad u(0)=u_0;\\
 {\rm (c)}\quad&
 u(t)=S_\nu(t)u_0-\int_0^tS_\nu(t-\tau)P c(\tau)\,d\tau
                 +\int_0^tS_\nu(t-\tau)r(\tau)\,d\tau;\\
 {\rm (d)}\quad&
 u(0)=u_0,\quad
 u(t)=S_\nu(t-s)u(s)-\int_s^tS_\nu(t-\tau)P c(\tau)\,d\tau
                 +\int_s^tS_\nu(t-\tau)r(\tau)\,d\tau
                 \quad(0\le s\le t\le T).
 \end{split}                                               \tag{50.16}
\]
In (a), p is necessarily q[u]; thus (b)--(d) reconstruct a unique
pair (u,p), not an arbitrary additive function of time in the pressure.

Proof. Since Pu=u and P is a fixed bounded Fourier multiplier,
\(Pu_t=u_t\) and \(P\Delta u=\Delta u\). Applying P to (a), with
\(P\nabla p=0\) and Pr=r, gives (b). Applying Q gives
\(\nabla p=-Qc\). Equation (50.15) and the zero pressure means force
p=q[u], since a periodic smooth function with zero gradient is constant.

Conversely, add (50.15) to the projected equation to obtain (a).
The source-term field \(g=-Pc+r\) is smooth, including all endpoint
time derivatives, by the bounded matrix multiplier and (50.6).
C59 applied with f=u, f0=u0, and this g proves (b)--(d).
All pointwise, L2, and Bochner equalities therefore refer to the same
actual smooth fields. The converse uses the stipulated smooth class;
no rough mild solution is silently promoted to that class.

50.2.2. Means and residual certification

Periodicity and div u=0 give
\[
 c_i=\partial_j(u_i u_j),\qquad \overline c=0,\qquad
 \overline{Pc}=P_0\overline c=0.
\]
Hence all equivalent predicates satisfy
\[
 \overline u(t)=\overline u_0+\int_0^t\overline r(\tau)\,d\tau.
                                                               \tag{50.17}
\]
In particular a nonzero velocity mean is retained. No mean-zero
assumption is needed for (50.16).

For every supplied smooth divergence-free v, define its actual
projected residual and its actual normalized pressure by
\[
 r_v=P\big(v_t+B(v,v)-\nu\Delta v\big),\qquad q_v=q[v].
                                                               \tag{50.18}
\]
Then \(Pr_v=r_v\), and all four predicates (50.16) hold with
\[
 (u,u_0,r,p)=(v,v(0),r_v,q_v).
\]
This follows by substituting (50.18) into (b), or directly by
\(v_t+B(v,v)+\nabla q_v-\nu\Delta v=r_v\).
Thus the mild residual identity is an exact identity for an
approximate trajectory, and
\[
 [\,r_v=0\text{ on }I\ \land\ v(0)=u_0\,]
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [\,(v,q_v)\in\mathscr E_\nu(u_0;T)\,].                    \tag{50.19}
\]
The actual datum equality in (50.19) is essential.

Setting r=0 identifies the normalized smooth classical solution set
with the projected and mild descriptions in (50.16); the existing
root bijections then identify the same members with the Newtonian
continuum, material, and Lagrange--d'Alembert descriptions. This
logical equivalence does not assert nonemptiness of those sets for
arbitrary three-dimensional data and T.

50.3. C61: two-time material transport of the Duhamel identity

50.3.1. Time-space typing and the actual propagator

First stipulate any smooth path \(\eta(t)\in
\operatorname{Diff}^\infty_{\mathrm{vol},0}(\Omega)\) with
\(\eta(0)=id\). Put
\[
 V_\eta=\eta_t,\quad F_t=D_a\eta(t),\quad A_t=F_t^{-1},
 \quad b(t)=V_\eta(t)\circ\eta(t)^{-1}.
\]
Here b is the velocity of the chosen coordinates. In the initial
linear transport statement b need not equal the field being
transported. Volume preservation gives div b=0.

Write \(\mathcal H_x\) for the Eulerian L2 copy and
\(\mathcal H_a^{(t)}\) for the material L2 copy at time t. These
material copies share the label measure da and the canonical
identification of vector components. Define
\[
 U_t:\mathcal H_x\longrightarrow\mathcal H_a^{(t)},\quad
 U_t h=h\circ\eta(t),\qquad U_t^{-1}H=H\circ\eta(t)^{-1}.
\]
Change of variables gives a surjective real linear isometry and
preservation of constants and means. Set
\[
 \mathcal S_t=U_t\mathcal H_\sigma,\quad
 P_t=U_tPU_t^{-1},\quad Q_t=I-P_t,
\]
\[
 \Delta_t=U_t\Delta U_t^{-1},\quad
 D(\Delta_t)=U_tH^2,\quad
 \mathcal C_tH=U_t[(b(t)\cdot\nabla)(U_t^{-1}H)]
             =(D_aH)A_tV_\eta(t)                         \tag{50.20}
\]
on the smooth material core. On that core
\(\Delta_tH=\operatorname{Div}_a(D_aH\,A_tA_t^{\mathsf T})\).
Restriction of \(-\Delta_t\) to \(\mathcal S_t\) is the closed
Stokes operator of C35, with domain \(U_tH^2_\sigma\).
The first-order expression \(\mathcal C_t\) is used on smooth
fields; it is not asserted to be a bounded L2 operator.

For \(0\le s\le t\le T\), define
\[
 \mathcal G_\eta(t,s):
       \mathcal H_a^{(s)}\longrightarrow\mathcal H_a^{(t)},
 \qquad
 \mathcal G_\eta(t,s)=U_tS_\nu(t-s)U_s^{-1}.                \tag{50.21}
\]
Its exact forward composition and norm identities are
\[
 \begin{split}
 \mathcal G_\eta(t,t)&=I_{\mathcal H_a^{(t)}},\\
 \mathcal G_\eta(t,s)\mathcal G_\eta(s,r)
       &=\mathcal G_\eta(t,r)\quad(0\le r\le s\le t\le T),\\
 \|\mathcal G_\eta(t,s)\|&=1,\\
 \|\mathcal G_\eta(t,s)|_{\mathcal H_{a,0}^{(s)}}\|
       &=e^{-\nu\lambda_1(t-s)},\\
 P_t\mathcal G_\eta(t,s)&=\mathcal G_\eta(t,s)P_s .
 \end{split}                                               \tag{50.22}
\]
The same sharp decay norm holds from \(\mathcal S_{s,0}\) to
\(\mathcal S_{t,0}\). It preserves the integral of a field and maps
constants to the same constants.

Proof. Substitute (50.21); the adjacent \(U_s^{-1}U_s\) factors cancel
and the Eulerian heat semigroup law supplies the forward composition.
The norm identities follow from the two isometries, (50.3)--(50.4),
and their respective extremizing constant or first-frequency vectors.
The intertwining identity follows from \(PS_\nu=S_\nu P\).
This is a two-time forward propagator between time-indexed spaces.
No inverse or backward heat operator is used. Smooth-density
approximation, strong continuity of heat, and continuity of
composition by \(\eta(t)\) on smooth fields also give strong joint
continuity of (50.21) on the closed triangle.

50.3.2. Both time derivatives and the transport term

For a fixed smooth Eulerian h and fixed smooth material H,
\[
 \partial_t(U_t h)=\mathcal C_tU_t h,\qquad
 \partial_t(U_t^{-1}H)=-(b(t)\cdot\nabla)(U_t^{-1}H).
                                                               \tag{50.23}
\]
The first identity is the ordinary chain rule. For the second,
differentiate \(\eta(t,\eta(t)^{-1}(x))=x\), obtaining
\(\partial_t\eta^{-1}=-(A_tV_\eta)\circ\eta^{-1}\), and apply
the spatial chain rule to \(H\circ\eta^{-1}\).
A time-dependent field receives its additional ordinary partial
time derivative. All component derivatives remain on the smooth
core; operator-norm differentiability of U_t is not used.

For a fixed smooth input H in the canonically identified material
label space, differentiating (50.21) gives
\[
 \partial_t[\mathcal G_\eta(t,s)H]
       =(\mathcal C_t+\nu\Delta_t)\mathcal G_\eta(t,s)H,
                                                               \tag{50.24}
\]
\[
 \partial_s[\mathcal G_\eta(t,s)H]
       =-\mathcal G_\eta(t,s)(\mathcal C_s+\nu\Delta_s)H.
                                                               \tag{50.25}
\]
For (50.24), the derivative of U_t contributes \(\mathcal C_t\),
and the derivative of the heat factor contributes
\(U_t\nu\Delta S_\nu(t-s)U_s^{-1}\). For (50.25), the derivative
of t-s contributes the negative heat derivative and the derivative
of \(U_s^{-1}\) contributes the second formula in (50.23).
Commutation of the Eulerian heat operator with \(\Delta\) places
these two terms in the order displayed in (50.25).
When H=H(s) varies, the right side receives
\(+\mathcal G_\eta(t,s)\partial_sH(s)\).

At t=s, (50.24) is the right t-derivative and (50.25) is the left
s-derivative whenever that direction lies in the triangle.
At the physical slab endpoints all derivatives are the admitted
one-sided derivatives. Uniform smooth convergence from C59 and
the bounded derivatives of \(\eta,\eta^{-1}\) on the compact slab
justify these limits. In particular the generator in (50.24)
contains both \(\mathcal C_t\) and \(\nu\Delta_t\).

For the exact test path \(\eta(t,a)=a+bt\) with constant b,
\[
 \mathcal G_\eta(t,s)H(a)
       =[S_\nu(t-s)H](a+b(t-s)),\qquad
 \mathcal C_t=b\cdot\nabla_a,\quad \Delta_t=\Delta_a.
                                                               \tag{50.26}
\]
A Fourier mode with \(k\cdot b\ne0\) acquires the factor
\(e^{2\pi i(k\cdot b)(t-s)}\) in addition to its heat multiplier.
This verifies directly the transport term in (50.24).
The fixed-configuration auxiliary semigroup of C37 and the present
physical two-time propagator therefore have distinct definitions.

50.3.3. Linear forced transport identity

For supplied smooth Eulerian h,g and smooth initial field h0, define
\[
 Y(t)=U_t h(t),\qquad G(t)=U_t g(t).
\]
The following statements, each with \(Y(0)=U_0h_0=h_0\), are equivalent:
\[
 h_t=\nu\Delta h+g,\qquad h(0)=h_0,                        \tag{50.27}
\]
\[
 Y_t=(\mathcal C_t+\nu\Delta_t)Y+G,                       \tag{50.28}
\]
\[
 Y(t)=\mathcal G_\eta(t,s)Y(s)+
                   \int_s^t\mathcal G_\eta(t,\tau)G(\tau)\,d\tau
                       \quad(0\le s\le t\le T).           \tag{50.29}
\]
For (50.27) iff (50.28), use the time-dependent version of (50.23):
\[
 Y_t=U_t h_t+\mathcal C_tY.
\]
For (50.27) implies (50.29), apply U_t to C59 and pass that fixed
bounded map through the interval integral. The exact integrand is
\[
 U_tS_\nu(t-\tau)g(\tau)
       =\mathcal G_\eta(t,\tau)U_\tau g(\tau).
\]
Conversely, apply the fixed \(U_t^{-1}\) to (50.29) at each t;
C59 recovers (50.27), and the chain rule gives (50.28).
Every factor \(U_\tau^{-1}U_\tau\) occurs at the same integration
time \(\tau\); replacing it by a different time would alter the identity.
All integrals take values in the common material label L2 space,
with output interpreted in its time-t copy. Smooth compact-slab
bounds identify these Bochner integrals with their pointwise values.

50.3.4. The actual nonlinear material mild equation

Now let u,r be as in C60, let \(\eta=\eta_u\) be the identity-normalized
flow of the supplied smooth u, and put
\[
 V=\eta_t=U_tu,\quad R(t)=U_t r(t),\quad
 \pi(t)=q[u](t)\circ\eta(t).
\]
Thus the coordinate velocity b equals u. In particular,
\[
 P_tV=V,\quad P_tR=R,\quad
 \mathcal C_tV=U_t B(u,u),\quad
 \overline\pi=0,\quad \|R(t)\|_2=\|r(t)\|_2.               \tag{50.30}
\]
The classical/projected/mild predicates of C60 are equivalent to
\[
 \boxed{\begin{split}
 V(t)={}&\mathcal G_\eta(t,s)V(s)\\
 &-\int_s^t\mathcal G_\eta(t,\tau)
                    P_\tau\mathcal C_\tau V(\tau)\,d\tau\\
 &+\int_s^t\mathcal G_\eta(t,\tau)R(\tau)\,d\tau
                         \qquad(0\le s\le t\le T),
 \end{split}}                                             \tag{50.31}
\]
together with \(\eta(0)=id\), \(V(0)=u_0\), and the stipulated flow
and volume-preservation relations. Indeed the Eulerian source in
C59 is \(g=-P B(u,u)+r\), whose material value is exactly
\[
 G=-P_t\mathcal C_tV+R.
\]
Substitution into (50.28)--(50.29) gives (50.31) and its exact
differential counterpart
\[
 \begin{split}
 V_t
  &=(\mathcal C_t+\nu\Delta_t)V-P_t\mathcal C_tV+R\\
  &=\nu\Delta_tV+Q_t\mathcal C_tV+R\\
  &=-\operatorname{grad}_{\eta(t)}\pi+\nu\Delta_tV+R .
 \end{split}                                               \tag{50.32}
\]
The last equality follows from
\(\nabla q[u]=-QB(u,u)\) and
\(\operatorname{grad}_{\eta}\pi=U_t\nabla q[u]\).

The tangential and normal equations are therefore
\[
 P_tV_t=\nu\Delta_tV+R,\qquad
 Q_tV_t=Q_t\mathcal C_tV=\dot P_tV
                 =-\operatorname{grad}_{\eta(t)}\pi.      \tag{50.33}
\]
The equality with \(\dot P_tV\) is the differentiated moving-tangency
identity of ID19: differentiate \(P_tV=V\), then use
\(P_t\dot P_tP_t=0\). The normal acceleration is retained.

For a converse beginning with a stipulated smooth volume-preserving
path eta, take \(u=V_\eta\circ\eta^{-1}\),
\(r=U_t^{-1}R\), and require \(P_tR=R\), the displayed initial data,
and (50.31) with V=V_eta. Apply \(U_t^{-1}\) to obtain (50.16);
then C60 reconstructs its unique normalized p=q[u], and
\(\pi=p\circ\eta\). The inverse initial and pressure conditions
follow because U_0=I and eta preserves volume. Thus both directions
are exact, with no independently prescribed trajectory omitted
from the hypotheses.

Integrating (50.32), or using (50.31) and the preserved mean, yields
\[
 \int_\Omega V(t,a)\,da
     =\overline u_0+\int_0^t\!\int_\Omega R(\tau,a)\,da\,d\tau .
                                                               \tag{50.34}
\]
To see the nonlinear term has zero mean, use
\(\int P_\tau\mathcal C_\tau V\,da
 =\int P B(u,u)\,dx=0\). Equation (50.22) transfers that zero
mean through each propagator, so (50.34) also follows directly
from the integral identity.

At each integration time, \(P_\tau\mathcal C_\tau V\) and R belong
to \(\mathcal S_\tau\); (50.22) sends them into \(\mathcal S_t\).
The Bochner integral therefore lies in the closed subspace
\(\mathcal S_t\). This is the exact moving tangency of (50.31).
The operator family \(\mathcal G_\eta\) depends on the supplied
trajectory; the nonlinear flow equation and its pressure constraint
have not been removed.

For r=0, (50.31)--(50.33) recover the original root equation and
its datum-preserving material bijection. For an approximate v,
use \(r_v\) and its own flow in (50.18), obtaining the exact material
residual formula. A trajectory required in these statements is
either explicitly supplied or is the unique flow of the supplied
smooth field on I, as proved in C01. No NSE trajectory is thereby
asserted to exist for arbitrary u0 and T.

  normalized torus. Instantiate the integrand with each component,
  |h|^2, and the pressure. The equalities give the mean, norm,
  inverse, and pressure-gauge transport used above.

  actual smooth component functions h(t,eta(t,a)) and

  differentiating eta(t,eta(t)^-1(x))=x. These substitutions give
  (50.20), (50.23), and the transport contributions in (50.24)--(50.25).
ML-N03/ML-N04:
  the bounded operator curve P_t from ID19 and the actual smooth
  curve V. Apply to P_tV=V, at interior times or within the physical
  time set. These endpoints are not applied to U_t as an
  operator-norm-differentiable L2 curve.
ML-E01:
  E=H_x,F=H_a, scalar field R, L=U_t fixed at the output time;
  integrand tau -> S_nu(t-tau)g(tau).
  For the converse use L=U_t^-1 at that same fixed t.
  For forward restart use L=G_eta(t,s) fixed in t,s.
  All codomains are complete; the integrands are continuous and
  therefore interval integrable on their compact intervals.
ML-E02:
  split the common time-t integral at s, with values in H_a and
  integrand tau -> G_eta(t,tau)G(tau). The proved smooth bounds
  give both required IntervalIntegrable premises.
ML-R01/ML-R02:
  component or L2 primitives on an interior time neighborhood or
  a closed finite interval, respectively. They encode the ordinary
  differentiated and integrated forms in (50.27)--(50.29).
  The actual endpoint derivatives are the direct one-sided limits
  justified after (50.25), consistently with ID26. No global
  positive-time or whole-line fluid extension is imported.

C61 and ID45 consist of (50.20)--(50.34) with both directions proved.
QED.

51.0. Exact common data

Let Omega=R^3/Z^3 have volume one, nu>0, and 0<T<infinity.
All fields in this section are real, periodic and jointly smooth on
I=[0,T], with the established one-sided endpoint convention.
Write B(a,b)=(a.grad)b, D a for the full spatial Jacobian,
S_a=(D a+D a^T)/2, and a^circ=a-mean(a).
The full-mean Leray projection has P_0=I and
P_k=I-kk^T/|k|^2 for k!=0. Put Q=I-P and lambda_1=4*pi^2.

For a smooth solenoidal velocity v, its normalized quadratic pressure
p[v] is the unique smooth mean-zero scalar with
  grad p[v]=-Q B(v,v).
Its existence, spatial/time regularity, reality and gauge follow from
the actual Fourier reconstruction in ID07/ID32.
Define the projected residual
  R(v)=v_t+P B(v,v)-nu Delta v.
Then
  R_E(v,p[v])=R(v),
  mean R(v)=d_t mean v,
  div R(v)=0.                                             (51.0)

No premise R(v)=0 is imposed in definitions or in C62.
All integrals in time have endpoints in I. The use of ordinary
derivatives is confined to interior times; finite-interval FTC and
continuity include both endpoints. Source all-positive-time tests are
handled only through the local extensions in ID17/ID26.

51.1.1. Actual bounded first-jet evaluation

At a fixed (t,x), set
  J_u=(D u,u), J_h=(D h,h), beta(M,y)=M y.
The spaces here are finite real Euclidean/operator spaces.
ML-B01 proves that beta is bounded bilinear. ML-B02 gives
  D beta(J_u)[J_h]=(D u)h+(D h)u
                  =B(h,u)+B(u,h).
ML-B03 gives the actual strict Frechet derivative of this same beta.
Direct bilinear expansion gives the exact equality
  beta(J_u+J_h)-beta(J_u)-D beta(J_u)[J_h]
     =(D h)h=B(h,h).                                      (51.1)

For the source field definition, M49 reads
  convection(v)(x)_i=sum_j v(x)_j coordinateDerivative(v,j)(x)_i.
Smoothness identifies its totalized fderiv with the actual derivative.
Expanding with v=u+h gives the same identity (51.1) componentwise.
Thus the jet map, the coordinate formula, and the periodic field
nonlinearity are explicitly identified.

This use of bounded bilinearity is pointwise and finite-dimensional.
No bounded map L2 x L2 -> L2 for PDE convection is asserted.

51.1.2. Symmetric pressure polarization

Define the scalar bilinear pressure K(a,b) by its actual Fourier series:
  K(a,b)_hat(0)=0,
  K(a,b)_hat(k)
    =-sum_{i,j}(k_i k_j/|k|^2)(a_i b_j)_hat(k), k!=0.      (51.2)
The sum over i,j is finite. The uniformly rapid Fourier estimates for
every spatial/time derivative give an actual jointly smooth real
periodic scalar. This follows by the same uniform differentiated-series
argument as ID07; no temporal regularity is inferred from a fixed-time
source conclusion alone.

The coefficient formula is bilinear. Interchanging i,j and using
a_i b_j=b_j a_i proves K(a,b)=K(b,a).
If c,d are spatial constants, solenoidality gives
  partial_i partial_j(c_i b_j+a_i d_j+c_i d_j)=0.
Thus K(a+c,b+d)=K(a,b), including when c,d depend smoothly on time.

For mixed transport c_ab=(B(a,b)+B(b,a))/2, direct differentiation gives
  div c_ab=partial_i partial_j(a_i b_j).
Indeed div a=div b=0 removes the second-derivative terms; the remaining
two sums agree after exchanging indices. Applying the scalar pressure
multiplier to c_ab gives precisely (51.2). M50 identifies these with
the actual Fourier integrals of infiniteTransportPressure(c_ab_hat).
M07--M09 then give
  grad K(a,b)=-Q[B(a,b)+B(b,a)]/2,
  mean K(a,b)=0.                                          (51.3)
For a=b this is p[a]=K(a,a). The zero pressure mode is fixed in every
identity, so there is no unrecorded additive function of time.

51.1.3. Exact residual and pressure expansions

Define the explicitly linear smooth-field operator
  L_u h=h_t+P[B(u,h)+B(h,u)]-nu Delta h.
Substituting (51.1) into R gives
  R(u+h)=R(u)+L_u h+P B(h,h).                              (51.4)
In particular, for every real epsilon,
  R(u+epsilon h)
    =R(u)+epsilon L_u h+epsilon^2 P B(h,h).                (51.5)

Define the pressure linearization q_u[h]=2K(u,h).
Bilinearity and symmetry of K give
  p[u+h]=p[u]+q_u[h]+p[h],
  p[u+epsilon h]
    =p[u]+epsilon q_u[h]+epsilon^2 p[h].                  (51.6)

These are identities of actual smooth fields on the entire finite slab.
They imply the actual directional derivatives along smooth affine
families; the interpretation does not require a Banach-space topology
on all smooth NSE trajectories.
For two directions h,k the mixed second variations are
  D^2 R[u](h,k)=P[B(h,k)+B(k,h)],
  D^2 p[u](h,k)=2K(h,k),                                  (51.7)
and all third affine variations vanish. For example subtracting the
four expansions at u+s h+t k, u+s h, u+t k and u leaves
s*t times the corresponding expression in (51.7). This proves the
second-variation assertions, including their factors.

The quadratic projected remainder is solenoidal and has zero mean:
  div(P B(h,h))=0, mean(P B(h,h))=0,
because div h=0 implies B(h,h)=div(h tensor h).
Consequently mean(L_u h)=d_t mean h. Means were not discarded by P.

51.1.4. Quantitative remainder norms

The operator estimate |(D h)h|<=|h| ||D h||op, projection contraction,
and spatial integration give
  ||P B(h,h)||_2<=||h||_infinity ||D h||_2.                 (51.8)
The norm on D h in the right side may be taken as the Frobenius L2 norm.
The full h is retained in (51.8): its constant mean can contribute the
solenoidal transport B(mean h,h^circ).

The scalar multiplier matrix kk^T/|k|^2 has Frobenius norm one.
Coefficient Cauchy--Schwarz and componentwise Parseval give
  ||K(a,b)||_2<=||a^circ tensor b^circ||_2
               <=||a^circ||_4 ||b^circ||_4.               (51.9)
Thus the exact pressure remainder obeys
  ||p[u+h]-p[u]-q_u[h]||_2<=||h^circ||_4^2.               (51.10)

For a mean-zero scalar f define
  ||f||_{dot H^-2}^2
    =sum_{k!=0}(4*pi^2|k|^2)^(-2)|f_hat(k)|^2,
  C_Omega^2=sum_{k!=0}(4*pi^2|k|^2)^(-2).                 (51.11)
On the dyadic shell 2^j<=|k|<2^(j+1), the number of lattice points is
at most a fixed constant times 2^(3j), while each weight is at most a
fixed constant times 2^(-4j). The resulting geometric sum proves
C_Omega<infinity.

Every Fourier coefficient of a^circ tensor b^circ has Frobenius norm
at most its L1 norm: pair the integral against a unit complex matrix,
use pointwise Cauchy--Schwarz, and use modulus one of the character.
Therefore
  ||K(a,b)||_{dot H^-2}
    <=C_Omega||a^circ tensor b^circ||_1
    <=C_Omega||a^circ||_2 ||b^circ||_2.                    (51.12)
This is the explicitly weighted negative norm, with no L1 boundedness
claim for the order-zero pressure operator.

51.2.1. Pressure and mean of the linearized field

Taking the full-mean Leray projection in (51.13) gives L_u z=0.
Subtract its pressure-free equation from (51.13); by (51.3),
  grad q=-Q[B(u,z)+B(z,u)]=grad q_u[z].
Both scalars have zero mean, so q=q_u[z]=2K(u,z).

Periodic integration gives
  mean B(u,z)=mean B(z,u)=mean grad q=mean Delta z=0.
For example B(u,z)_i=partial_j(u_j z_i), since div u=0;
the other term uses div z=0. Thus
  mean z(t)=mean z0=:m_z, mean u(t)=mean u0=:m_u.           (51.14)

Set
  v^epsilon=u+epsilon z,
  p_app^epsilon=p[v^epsilon]
               =p+epsilon q+epsilon^2 p[z],
  f_z=P B(z,z).                                          (51.15)
Equations (51.5)--(51.6) prove the actual normalized residual equation
  v_t^epsilon+B(v^epsilon,v^epsilon)+grad p_app^epsilon
          -nu Delta v^epsilon
       =epsilon^2 f_z,                                   (51.16)
with div f_z=0 and mean f_z=0.

If the pressure is instead truncated at first order,

The distinction between (51.16) and (51.18) is exact: the added pressure
epsilon^2 p[z] changes the residual by -epsilon^2 Q B(z,z).
No pressure correction is silently omitted in the projected certificate.

51.2.2. Explicit uniform comparison constants

Define continuous nonnegative functions from u,z only:
  a_u(t)=max_{x,|xi|=1}[-xi^T S_u(t,x)xi],
  s_z(t)=||S_z(t)||_{infinity,op},
  a_*(t)=a_u(t)+epsilon_star s_z(t),
  alpha_*(t)=a_*(t)-nu lambda_1,
  b(t)=||f_z(t)||_2.
The trace-zero condition gives a_u>=0, as in ID33.
Compactness and the operator-norm comparison of symmetric matrices
give continuity of these maxima. At every allowed epsilon,
  a_{v^epsilon}(t)<=a_*(t).

Set
  E_*(t,s)=exp(integral_s^t alpha_*(r) dr),
  C_*(t)=integral_0^t E_*(t,s)b(s) ds.                     (51.19)
Thus C_*>=0, C_*(0)=0 and C_*'=alpha_* C_*+b.
All constants are finite and depend only on the given u,z,nu,T and
epsilon_star. No derivative norm of u^epsilon appears.

For b_*=sup_I b and A_*=integral_0^T a_*,

  C_*^{max}<=b_* exp(A_*)[1-exp(-nu lambda_1 T)]/(nu lambda_1).

Indeed E_*(t,s)=exp(integral_s^t a_*)exp(-nu lambda_1(t-s))
and a_*>=0. This bound retains the unit-torus spectral gap.
The exact integral (51.19) is the primary certificate.

51.2.3. Complete error identity and second-order estimate

Let
  w^epsilon=u^epsilon-v^epsilon,
  Y=||w^epsilon||_2^2, G=||D w^epsilon||_2.
Subtracting (51.16) from the exact equation gives
  w_t+B(u^epsilon,w)+B(w,v^epsilon)
       +grad(p^epsilon-p_app^epsilon)-nu Delta w
    =-epsilon^2 f_z.                                     (51.21)
The initial error is zero. By (51.17), mean w=0 at every time.

Pairing with w, using div u^epsilon=div w=0 and periodic integration,
gives the actual identity
  (1/2)Y'+nu G^2
    =-integral w^T S_{v^epsilon}w-epsilon^2<f_z,w>.         (51.22)
The unknown exact velocity transports w, and that mixed transport term
cancels. The retained strain is the known approximate strain.
Full mean-zero Parseval gives G^2>=lambda_1 Y, so
  (1/2)Y'<=alpha_* Y+epsilon^2 b sqrt(Y).                  (51.23)

For completeness the scalar comparison is valid even when alpha_*<0.
For delta>0 put y_delta=sqrt(Y+delta^2). Direct differentiation gives
  y_delta'<=alpha_* y_delta+epsilon^2 b+delta|alpha_*|.
Multiplication by exp(-integral_0^t alpha_*) and finite-interval FTC
give an integrated inequality. The initial value is y_delta(0)=delta.
The correction is bounded by
delta*T*exp(T||alpha_*||infinity)||alpha_*||infinity,
which tends to zero. Letting delta decrease to zero proves
  ||u^epsilon(t)-u(t)-epsilon z(t)||_2
     <=epsilon^2 C_*(t), 0<=t<=T.                         (51.24)
No differentiation of the norm at a zero is used.

For epsilon!=0 this also gives
  ||(u^epsilon-u)/epsilon-z||_{L_infinity(I;L2)}
     <=|epsilon| C_*^{max}.                              (51.25)
This is an implication for the supplied exact solutions.
If a family satisfying the displayed hypotheses is provided, (51.25)
gives its directional difference-quotient limit along those parameters.
It does not construct such a family or assert a global solution map.

51.2.4. Integrated dissipation estimate

Return to the unabsorbed identity (51.22) and insert (51.24):
  (1/2)Y(t)+nu integral_0^t G(s)^2 ds
    <=epsilon^4 integral_0^t
          [a_*(s)C_*(s)^2+b(s)C_*(s)] ds.                 (51.26)
Define

It is nonnegative and finite. With the convention

The integrated derivative estimate follows from the actual energy
identity; it is not an interpolation inference from L2 convergence.

51.2.5. Pressure certificate in the precise negative norm

All pressures below have zero spatial mean. Define
  N_*(t)=||u^circ(t)||_2+epsilon_star||z^circ(t)||_2.
Then ||(v^epsilon)^circ||_2<=N_* and the centered exact/approximate

   <=C_Omega[2N_*+epsilon^2 C_*]epsilon^2 C_*.              (51.28)
For clarity, this follows from

  ||a||_2<=||b||_2+||w||_2,
with a=(u^epsilon)^circ and b=(v^epsilon)^circ, followed by the

51.3.3. Actual reference infinitesimal material fields

  W_t=M W+z o eta, W(0)=0, M=(D u) o eta,
  Z=W_t, Z(0)=z0,
  rho=q o eta+[(grad p) o eta].W.                         (51.37)
The explicit solution is
  W(t)=F(t) integral_0^t A(s)[z(s) o eta(s)]ds,
with F=D_a eta, A=F^(-1).
Differentiation using F_t=M F and A_t=-A M verifies the ODE and initial
value. Finite linear uniqueness verifies agreement with Section49.
The scalar rho is the actual material pressure variation; it is not
replaced by q o eta alone.

Let
  xi^epsilon=chi_tilde^epsilon-eta_tilde,
  gamma^epsilon=xi^epsilon-epsilon W.
Set the finite reference functions
  Z_infinity(t)=||z(t)||infinity,
  H_u(t)=sup_x ||D^2u(t,x)||_{bilinear,op},
  d_1(t)=integral_0^t exp(integral_s^t L_u) Z_infinity(s)ds.
The exact flow difference satisfies
  xi_t=u(t,eta+xi)-u(t,eta)+epsilon z(t,eta+xi).
The spatial Lipschitz bound therefore gives
  ||xi^epsilon(t)||infinity<=|epsilon| d_1(t).             (51.38)
The lift notation inside the compositions is understood; all
Eulerian fields are evaluated through their periodic lifts.

51.3.4. Quantitative second-order reference flow remainder

Two applications of one-dimensional FTC give the vector Taylor identity
  u(x+d)-u(x)-D u(x)d
    =integral_0^1(1-s)D^2u(x+s d)[d,d]ds.
Hence its norm is at most H_u |d|^2/2.
Subtract epsilon times (51.37) from the exact xi equation:
  gamma_t=M gamma
     +[u(eta+xi)-u(eta)-D u(eta)xi]
     +epsilon[z(eta+xi)-z(eta)].                          (51.39)
Thus the nonhomogeneous part has pointwise norm at most
  epsilon^2[H_u d_1^2/2+L_z d_1].

Define
  d_2(t)=integral_0^t exp(integral_s^t L_u)
                      [H_u(s)d_1(s)^2/2+L_z(s)d_1(s)]ds,
  k_2(t)=L_u(t)d_2(t)+H_u(t)d_1(t)^2/2+L_z(t)d_1(t).
A pointwise integrating-factor comparison, followed by supremum over
the label torus, proves
  ||chi_tilde^epsilon-eta_tilde-epsilon W||infinity
       <=epsilon^2 d_2(t),
  ||V_app^epsilon-V-epsilon Z||infinity
       <=epsilon^2 k_2(t).                               (51.40)
The velocity bound follows directly from (51.39), not by differentiating
the inequality for positions. The scalar coefficients are continuous
and finite because the supplied u,z are smooth on the compact slab.

Combining (51.36) with (51.40), and using volume(Omega)=1, yields
  ||eta_tilde^epsilon-eta_tilde-epsilon W||_2
       <=epsilon^2[D_*(t)+d_2(t)],
  ||V_exact^epsilon-V-epsilon Z||_2
       <=epsilon^2[C_*(t)+L_*(t)D_*(t)+k_2(t)].             (51.41)
These are the actual infinitesimal-to-finite material position and
velocity estimates. They give no C1 estimate on the exact perturbed
flow; the derivative information used for the Taylor step belongs only
to the explicitly known reference fields u,z.

51.3.5. Pressure scope and material pressure expansion

For the known reference ansatz, every term is smooth with explicit
reference bounds. Set
  G_p=||grad p||infinity, H_p=||D^2p||infinity,op,
  G_q=||grad q||infinity, P_z=||p[z]||infinity,
  p_2=G_p d_2+H_p d_1^2/2+G_q d_1+P_z.
Expanding p(t,eta+xi) to second order, q(t,eta+xi) to first order,
and retaining the exact epsilon^2 p[z] term gives
  ||pi_app^epsilon-pi-epsilon rho||infinity
       <=epsilon^2 p_2(t).                               (51.42)
The contribution G_p d_2 comes from the actual position remainder gamma,
and the term G_q d_1 comes from epsilon[q(eta+xi)-q(eta)].
This proves the reference pressure expansion with rho as in (51.37).

Without any extra exact-solution bound, an aligned negative-norm
certificate remains available. For a mean-zero smooth material scalar H
define, at the exact flow,
  ||H||_{dot H^-2,eta^epsilon}
      :=||H o (eta^epsilon)^(-1)||_{dot H^-2}.             (51.43)
This is the explicitly transported norm, with the Fourier weights
in (51.11), not a fixed-label Sobolev norm.
Composition gives
  pi_exact^epsilon-pi_app^epsilon o theta^epsilon
       =(p^epsilon-p_app^epsilon) o eta^epsilon,
so (51.28) implies
  ||pi_exact^epsilon-pi_app^epsilon o theta^epsilon||
                      _{dot H^-2,eta^epsilon}
    <=C_Omega[2N_*+epsilon^2 C_*]epsilon^2 C_*.             (51.44)
The zero mean is retained by volume preservation on both sides.

If the ADDITIONAL uniform L-infinity premise (51.30) is supplied, an
unweighted material L2 pressure conclusion follows separately.
Let
  G_app,*(t)=G_p(t)+epsilon_star G_q(t)
                    +epsilon_star^2||grad p[z](t)||infinity.
Then grad p_app^epsilon has norm at most G_app,*.
Split the same-label pressure difference as
  pi_exact^epsilon-pi_app^epsilon
    =(p^epsilon-p_app^epsilon) o eta^epsilon
       +p_app^epsilon o eta^epsilon-p_app^epsilon o chi^epsilon.
The first term has its Eulerian L2 norm; the second is bounded by
G_app,*||delta^epsilon||_2. Equations (51.31) before adding p[z],
(51.36), and (51.42) give
  ||pi_exact^epsilon-pi-epsilon rho||_2
   <=epsilon^2{
       [M_*+N_infinity,*]C_*+G_app,*D_*+p_2 }.              (51.45)
Premise (51.30) and boundedness of its coefficient remain explicit.
No unweighted pressure rate is inferred solely from the velocity L2
certificate.

51.4. Exact composition and implementation boundary

The mathematical composition is
  bounded finite evaluation + actual convection coefficients
      -> C62 / ID46;
  stipulated base + stipulated linearized pair + ID46
      -> exact ansatz residual and its changed initial datum;
  any supplied exact root at that same datum + ID33 + ID46
      -> C63 / ID47;
  actual smooth flows + residual conjugacy + ID35
      + the explicit reference Taylor integral
      -> C64 / ID48.

The three pending Lean groups can be divided into independent exact
implementation edges without changing the already proved mathematics:

L46.a: finite first-jet evaluation and actual convection polarization.
L46.b: symmetric normalized mixed pressure and constant-mode cancellation.
L46.c: exact first/second residual and pressure variations.
L46.d: projected-remainder L2 bound and pressure L2/H-minus-two bounds.

L47.a: linearized pressure uniqueness and mean ledger.
L47.b: exact affine ansatz residual and full normalized pressure.
L47.c: known-strain error identity and mean-zero spectral gap.
L47.d: regularized norm, negative coefficient, and variable integrating factor.
L47.e: exact integrated dissipation estimate.
L47.f: normalized pressure negative-norm certificate.
L47.g: optional L2 pressure estimate with its additional uniform premise.

L48.a: exact forced material ansatz equation and residual norm.
L48.b: aligned material velocity identity.
L48.c: canonical lift feedback and same-label L2 estimates.
L48.d: reference W,Z reconstruction with literal Z=W_t.
L48.e: quantitative reference second-order Taylor remainder.
L48.f: exact material position/velocity composition.
L48.g: reference pressure variation, transported negative norm,
       and the separately conditional unweighted pressure estimate.

No source endpoint is promoted by this decomposition.
No local or external Lean execution, CI invocation, or repository mutation
has been performed for these identities.
The root C11, its pressure gauges, its initial data, and its finite smooth
solution classes remain unchanged. Perturbed data are explicitly named
u0+epsilon z0. The exact solutions used in C63--C64 are supplied on the
common slab; the derivation asserts no existence, continuation, or
global differentiability of an NSE solution map.

PRECISE_SPECIALIZATIONS:
1. C59 / (50.10):
   𝕜=ℝ, E=the actual real vector L2 space H, F=ℂ with its real
   normed-space structure, μ=Lebesgue volume on ℝ, a=s, b=t.
   L is one fixed component Fourier coefficient at k:
     L(h)=∫_Omega exp(-2*pi*i*k dot x)*h_i(x) dx.
   Linearity follows from the integral; the bound
     |L(h)|<=||h_i||_2<=||h||_2
   follows from Cauchy--Schwarz and volume(Omega)=1. This constructs
   its actual bounded real-linear map. The integrand is
     f(tau)=S_nu(t-tau)g(tau).
   Strong continuity on [s,t] proves IntervalIntegrable.
   The output is exactly the coefficient/integral commutation (50.10).

2. C59 / restart in (50.11), and C60:
   E=F=H, 𝕜=ℝ, L=S_nu(t-s), with s,t fixed;
   f(tau)=S_nu(s-tau)g(tau) on [0,s].
   The semigroup identity converts L(f(tau)) to
     S_nu(t-tau)g(tau).
   Together with ML-E02 this proves the exact restart formula.
   L=P gives the corresponding passage through the projected integral.

3. C61 / (50.29):
   E=H_x, F=H_a, 𝕜=ℝ, L=U_t at fixed output time t;
   f(tau)=S_nu(t-tau)g(tau), a=s, b=t.
   The output is the exact identity
     U_t(∫_s^t S_nu(t-tau)g(tau) d tau)
       =∫_s^t G_eta(t,tau)U_tau g(tau) d tau,
   using U_tau^-1 U_tau=I at the same tau.
   The converse uses L=U_t^-1, again fixed at the output time.
   A material restart can use L=G_eta(t,s), fixed in t,s.

ADAPTER_BOUNDARY:
The source theorem moves one fixed bounded linear map through an
already integrable Bochner integral. It does not differentiate U_t,
establish regularity of the nonlinear term, construct a flow, or
provide the heat multiplier. Those identities are derived in ID43--ID45.
Completeness, actual coefficient maps, and interval-integrability
instances must be supplied in the Lean adapter; the mathematical
constructions and bounds are present in Section 50.

theorem smoothFourierSynthesis_laplacian_coeff (c : FourierCoeff)
    (hc : ∀ i : Fin 3, RapidScalarFourier (fun k => c k i))
    (hreal : SpectralReality c) :
    datumFourierCoeff (laplacian (smoothFourierSynthesis c)) = laplacianCoefficient c

IMPORTED_TYPE_INTERPRETATION:
FourierCoeff = (Fin 3 -> Z) -> Fin 3 -> C.
Field = Vec -> Vec.
RapidScalarFourier b states, for every natural m, summability of
  k -> ||b k|| * ||fourierPhaseCLM k||^m.
SpectralReality c states c(-k,i)=star(c(k,i)).
The physical coefficient/synthesis and torus/unit-cube identifications
are the actual constructions already used by M24 and ID16/Section 44.0.

PRECISE_SPECIALIZATIONS:
1. For supplied smooth periodic f and fixed h>=0, put
     c(k,i)=exp(-nu*4*pi^2*|k|^2*h)*datumFourierCoeff(f)(k,i).
   The scalar multiplier is real, even in k, and lies in [0,1].
   Therefore SpectralReality follows from that of the actual real f,
   and each required moment is bounded by the corresponding finite
   RapidScalarFourier moment of f. Those moments follow from the
   explicit smooth coefficient decay in (50.6).
   M24 realizes c as the coefficient family of the actual smooth
   heat synthesis. M48 gives the exact physical Laplacian coefficient
     -4*pi^2*|k|^2*c(k,i).
   This closes the synthesis-to-differential-operator interface in
   (50.2),(50.5) and the smooth heat derivative.

2. At fixed 0<=s<=t<=T, take c(k,i)=d_k(t,s)_i from (50.7).
   Uniform rapid decay (50.6)--(50.9) proves the required moments.
   The integrand's conjugate symmetry gives SpectralReality after
   the real time integral. M48 then identifies the actual Laplacian
   of the constructed Duhamel field.
   M24 and Fourier uniqueness identify that field with the Bochner
   integral in (50.10).

ADAPTER_BOUNDARY:
There is no SpectralMeanZero or SpectralSolenoidal premise in this
declaration; constant modes are included. It establishes an exact
coefficient identity for a smooth synthesis. It does not by itself
supply an actual heat semigroup, interchange time derivatives with
an infinite Fourier sum, or prove Duhamel or nonlinear existence.
All those mathematical interfaces used here are proved in ID43;
their Lean implementations remain L43.

The source proof uses existing M31 and M24. Its distinct declared
name was absent from the v1.4 source index. This register adds that
actual source corollary once; it does not assign new IDs to either
already indexed input declaration.
